=== PUCT PROJECT 58481 Tract Comments FINAL.pdf ===
                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §                   BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §
                                                 §                     OF TEXAS


    TRACT HOLDING COMPANY I, LLC’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S
 PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
                      STANDARDS (“STANDARDS”)

I.     Introduction

         Tract Holding Company I, LLC, on behalf of its affiliates, (“Tract”) appreciates the
opportunity to submit comments on key issues addressed in this rulemaking. Tract, through its
affiliates, acquires land and develops construction-ready development sites for data centers—pre-
positioning power, fiber, zoning, and entitlements—to execute the most difficult early-state
development work which provides data center constructors with faster build cycles at lower risk.
Tract is actively developing several such projects in Texas and currently has 2.8 gigawatts (“GW”)
of proposed projects, representing an ultimate capacity of 6.2 GW, in advanced stages of
development in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) Large Load Interconnection
Study (“LLIS”) process (comprised of four projects across three Transmission Service Providers
(“TSPs”)), with more in development. Tract appreciates the PUCT’s process thus far and supports
several changes made by the PUCT, however, Tract identifies several issues below that make the
rule legally vulnerable or conflict with enacting legislation. Tract’s affiliate, Fleet Data Centers,
recently announced a lease in Nevada with a AA- investment grade rated tenant with a market cap
in excess of $3 trillion and would like to bring similar business development to Texas.

II.    Applicability

        Tract requests the Commission clarify that these Standards only apply to new large load
requests submitted to TSPs after the effective date of the rule. Projects with executed agreements
with TSPs prior to the rule becoming effective, and whose financial parameters were set under
existing rules, should not be negatively impacted by the retroactive application of this rule. As
discussed during the Texas House State Affairs Committee Meeting April 9, 2026, projects with
commitments in hand were not intended to be the target of this new rule. Through Senate Bill 6
(2025 Reg. Ses.) (“SB 6”), the Texas Legislature and Governor evinced their intent by explicitly
stating that “the standards must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded
interconnection.” Texas Utilities Code § 37.0561(c). This plain language would require the new
Standards be applied only to projects requesting “new or expanded” interconnection after the date
of adoption of the rule implementing the statute. The plain language of SB 6 also states that these

                                                 1
 are Standards the PUCT must implement by rule; they are not requirements applicable as of the
effective date of the underlying bill (i.e. June 20, 2025) or some other date (e.g. September 1, 2025,
which is a date applicable to the net metering review requirements). Texas Utilities Code §
37.0561(b).

        When serious projects begin the process of entering the ERCOT market, significant
decisions, including financial resource commitments, are made based on the rules in place at the
time. To change these rules for projects already in advanced stages of development will have a
negative impact on businesses and send a harmful market signal that will deter future business
development and will create overall regulatory uncertainty, counter to the intent of SB 6. If the
Commission believes it must apply these Standards to existing load interconnection requests,
contrary to the plain language of SB 6, the new Standards adopted by this rule should not apply to
projects that are so far along that they have already been assigned an LLIS number by ERCOT, or
have studies submitted to ERCOT by the TSP, or at the very least have executed agreements with
the TSP to provide financial security or contributions. Without such clarification, this rule could
conflict with executed agreements, change terms of existing contracts, and therefore be subject to
judicial challenge by an aggrieved counterparty. Upsetting contractual relationships should be a
last resort.

        Moreover, applying these Standards only to newly submitted requests after the adoption
date has the added benefit of avoiding confusion with the ongoing Batch Study Process ERCOT
is developing through PGRR145. The Batch Zero criteria and batching process will be applied to
both existing and new requests going forward, while these Standards would apply only to new
requests submitted after the Standards are adopted. Doing so avoids confusion and reduces the
burden and complexity faced by developers, utilities, PUCT, and ERCOT that would result if
existing requests are required to meet the Batch requirements by July in addition to these Standards
whenever they become effective. In light of the above, Tract respectfully recommends changes to
the applicability section of the Standards to reflect the rule only applies to requests submitted to a
TSP after the effective date of this rule.

        In contrast, retroactively introducing new burdens on late-stage projects imposes additional
costs, can create delays, and will potentially harm businesses, strand investment, and discourage
future investment in the state, contrary to the goals of SB 6. This rulemaking process itself should
not become a cause of delay in projects moving forward. Tract is especially concerned that the
new rule imposes costs or burdens on projects previously studied or in the process of being studied
and most certainly for those projects that have already executed agreements with TSPs on the basis
of the old rules.

       Thus, Tract also respectfully recommends changes to sections addressing financial security
to recognize the contributions and financial securities provided by projects to date. As Chairman
Gleason himself noted at the House State Affairs Committee Meeting, projects with existing
agreements with their TSPs under that have provided financial security or contributions will have

                                                  2
 to be treated differently than those that have not. Specifically, we recommend netting the newly
imposed requirements against already provided security and contributions. This is the only way to
avoid double-securing the same costs, which would deter business development without protecting
against any incremental risks and depart significantly from cost-causation principles. Indeed, SB6
contemplates a uniform security amount that should apply to any project seeking interconnection
to ERCOT. Netting new requirements against already provided security ensures a uniform entry
gate, whereas if not netted, those early businesses who acted responsibly to secure utility costs
ahead of requirements to do so will be subject to newly imposed uniform requirements in addition
to already provided security and contributions. This would discriminate against and penalize
projects initiated prior to the rule’s adoption that took prior action to protect the TSP’s customers
from stranded costs.


III.   Remove non-refundable fee
        Imposing a non-refundable fee that is not tied to the costs to interconnect violates cost
causation principles and will limit economic growth. Because the proposed non-refundable fee is
not required until the Interconnection Agreement step, this fee will not address the gating issue
against phantom loads. Furthermore, SB6 authorizes the PUCT to include all or some combination
of refundable financial security related to the size of the project ($/MW), contributions in aid of
construction (“CIAC”) for direct connection costs, and security for long-lead-time equipment
outlays by the interconnecting utility. SB6 does not point to any non-refundable fees. Although it
gives the Commission additional authority in §37.0561(h)(4) to adopt additional measures
“acceptable to the commission,” this does not license the Commission to depart from cost-
causation principles that are rooted in PURA.

        A uniform $/MW non-refundable fee departs from cost-causation in at least two ways.
First, given all of the securities and contributions required by the rule already, the fee cannot be
reasonably related to costs as those have already been secured by the large load through other
measures. The fee is in addition to costs. Second, a uniform fee cannot reasonably be related to
actual costs as costs vary significantly with respect to required transmission upgrades across large
loads depending on size, timing, location, and many other factors. Because SB6 does not authorize
this fee and because it is not rationally related to cost-causation, the non-refundable fee exceeds
the PUCT’s authority. The non-refundable fee also makes the refundability provision of SB6
superfluous by converting the security remaining after costs into the fee. If all of the security
provided gets converted into a fee, the refundability provisions of SB6 will have no meaning. Thus,
adding the requirement for a non-refundable fee to the Standards makes the proposed rule
vulnerable to legal challenge, creating additional perceived risk for investors and regulatory and
possibly judicial uncertainty, which will negatively impact investment.
        Instead, tying required fees and security amounts to costs caused by the large load ensures
equity and prevents uneconomic projects from moving forward, thereby minimizing stranded costs
and maintaining reliability. A flat non-refundable fee does not send a price signal to the

                                                 3
 development market but rather signals a lack of support for business development. If a non-
refundable fee is adopted, it should provide some value to the large load customer, such as a
transmission service bill credit, tax credit, or some other item of value.
       At the March 24, 2026, ERCOT Batch Study Process workshop, in response to opposition
to PUCT’s proposed non-refundable interconnection fee, Barksdale English indicated the PUCT
would consider counter-proposals from stakeholders that: (1) minimize stranded costs; and (2)
reduce phantom loads. Tract proposes:

      1. Minimize Stranded Costs -
            a. By requiring CIAC for direct connection costs, AND $/MW security for LLE, AND
               security for long-lead-time equipment, AND security for system upgrades, this
               proposed rule already minimizes if not eliminates stranded cost risk.

              b. The direct connection and system upgrade contributions and securities alone should
                 pay for any costs imposed by the large load on other ratepayers. Nevertheless, out
                 of an abundance of caution, any lingering stranded cost risk can be mitigated
                 through the proposed dollar per megawatt refundable security, which is on top of
                 actual costs identified by the utilities necessary to interconnect the large load.
                 Minimum transmission charges, as recommended by Google and Lancium (based
                 on 25% of non-coincident peak demand), could be a method to further insulate
                 against stranded cost risk in the transmission cost allocation rulemaking.

              c. The proper venue for any further perceived transmission cost risk can be addressed
                 in Project 58484, Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery, as required by Section
                 6 of SB6. Recent reports suggest that large load growth can reduce rates for other
                 customers.1 This was corroborated by Oncor's witness at the State Affairs
                 Committee Hearing who testified that for every $143 in transmission costs caused
                 by large loads they collect $146 in revenue. At that hearing, Vistra also asserted
                 that load growth would benefit its gas fleet through higher utilization. Spreading
                 fixed costs over higher volumes should lead to lower rates, which the PUCT can
                 evaluate in Project 58484.

      2. Reduce Phantom Loads –
            a. To deter phantom loads, the PUCT should require a deed or lease at the
               Interconnection Agreement stage. A purchase and sale agreement (“PSA”) is
               insufficient to demonstrate a sufficiently serious project because a PSA is an
               executory contract where the title to the land required to construct the project does
               not pass to the buyer until the deed is delivered at closing. A project has more at
               stake and is committed to the land once it has deed in hand, which conveys the fee
               simple estate needed for full control and financing. PSAs have provisions allowing

1
    https://emp.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-03/Retail%20Price%20Trends_2026%20edition.pdf.

                                                      4
               buyer or seller to terminate, not so for a deed. PSAs can be terminated based on
              due diligence, lack of financing, inspection, environmental, zoning, title defects, or
              any other mutually agreed condition. Other legal remedies like those for fraud or
              rescission could also apply to terminate or invalidate a PSA. This could lead to a
              scenario where a project is reserved or allocated interconnection capacity by
              ERCOT but is unable to construct the load consuming facilities because it lacks the
              legal authority to enter, possess, or construct on the land. Even if there were no
              legal concerns, practically speaking, projects that are seeking to energize in the next
              few years are less likely to do so if they did not have a lease or deed by the time of
              interconnection agreement execution.

           b. The PUCT should consider requiring demonstration of sufficient local zoning
              approvals needed to construct the large load. This could take the form of proof of
              approved zoning uses, development agreements with Authorities Having
              Jurisdiction (“AHJs”), or letters of no zoning required from county judges. TSPs
              are familiar with local zoning requirements, albeit for different uses, and can
              determine whether a large load has demonstrated sufficient local zoning approvals
              required to construct the large load, or proof that no such approvals are required.
              This would address PUCT’s concern about phantom loads while at the same time
              ensure that loads meeting the PUCT’s new standards have sufficient local buy-in to
              receive approvals subject to local input. Tract therefore suggests the following
              language to the proposed rule:
                      Before executing an Interconnection Agreement under this Section, an
                      officer or official with binding authority over the large load customer shall
                      attest and provide documentation to the TSP demonstrating that the large
                      load has the local zoning approvals required to construct the large load, or
                      that local zoning approvals are not required.

IV.    Guide ERCOT on Batch Zero treatment for late-stage legacy interconnect loads

        At the February 6th, 2026 PUCT Open Meeting, ERCOT clearly stated that while the
ERCOT Batch Study workshop and ERCOT revision request process is underway, the existing
Planning Guide remains in effect. Tract has been moving forward with this understanding for its
projects, investing significant capital and time to bring these projects to Texas.
       a. ERCOT’s March 17th comments introduced an earlier cutoff date for completion of
          studies for Interconnecting Large Load Entities (“ILLEs”) to qualify for Batch Zero
          base load treatment. The dates used are unjustified, violate PUCT guidance, result in
          waste, and provide no effective notice. In its March 17 comments, ERCOT’s provided
          justification for the March 4 date is for complete and valid LLIS studies rather than
          RPG studies. Even if the LLIS justification was also intended to encompass RPG
          studies, the date the PGRR was published is not a relevant or justified cutoff. In the

                                                5
         March 24 workshop, ERCOT expressed concern with a late deluge of submitted studies
        that could invalidate or “jump ahead” of earlier submitted studies. This concern is
        misplaced, as the deadline to submit the studies in question would remain in December
        of 2025, well before the PGRR was published, preventing a deluge of any kind.

     b. By setting a cutoff date for complete and valid studies that is before PGRR 145 takes
        effect, ERCOT is violating prior guidance. Existing Planning Guide 3.1.1.3 requires
        utilities to submit studies to RPG for acceptance. ILLEs and utilities relied on those
        sections and properly submitted studies to RPG by the end of last year. The RPG
        timeline for submission and approval/endorsement is out of an ILLE’s control, and
        even if it were in its control, it could not today meet the cutoff proposed by ERCOT, as
        it is in the past. This retroactive cutoff of an existing required process undermines
        confidence in the resulting process and does not support business development. ILLEs,
        utilities, RPG stakeholders, and ERCOT itself have invested significant time and
        resources into following existing Planning Guide processes. Those efforts may be
        wasted for large loads that, despite submitting to utilities several years ago and having
        contributions and securities in place, were not approved or endorsed by RPG by March
        4th. Instead, the PUCT should guide ERCOT that large loads included in any RPG
        studies approved by July 10 should be in Batch Zero Base.

     c. Intake of Batch Zero Base Load requests in July 2026 need to be completed through
        the Batch Zero Process. However, once ERCOT determines studies are valid and
        proposed Section 9.2.1.4(3) has been satisfied, those projects should not have to wait
        for the Batch Study to be completed or any other approvals or agreements beyond those
        a large load would have to complete under the Legacy process (e.g. Approval to
        Energize). PUCT should guide ERCOT that any such projects can proceed without any
        further Batch Study-related approvals or studies.
     d. Thus, PUCT should guide ERCOT such that:
             i. Large loads in studies submitted by December 31, 2025 and accepted by July
                10, 2026 will be considered Bath Zero Base Load.
            ii. A large load, which is validated by its TSP as having contributed to the
                justification for an approved RPG project, which is now part of the RTP going
                forward, and which met all currently applicable requirements including
                associated fees and security, shall not be subject to additional study, and be
                modeled in the Batch Study at no less than what was studied or contracted, and
                should proceed under the legacy process. This is consistent with both the
                direction of the PUCT on February 6, and ERCOT’s answers to questions at the
                March 10, 2026 workshop and is supportive of business development without
                stranding costs or jeopardizing reliability.

V.   Guide ERCOT on Large Loads whose Studies are invalidated by ERCOT


                                              6
         If PUCT adopts a non-refundable fee, the non-refundable fee should not apply to large
loads that are seeking to enter Batch Zero as base load, but could apply to those large loads whose
studies are invalidated by ERCOT. After a project submits the non-refundable fee in July as base
load, ERCOT may, in August, deem the studies associated with a project invalid. In contrast, large
loads entering the Batch Zero process in July as Studied Load will not be required to post non-
refundable fees until they have received fixed capacity allocation commitments through the
ERCOT process. At the March 24, 2026 Batch Zero workshop, ERCOT acknowledged this issue
and stated that it was considering changes. Failure to resolve this mismatch of funding and
commitment could result in huge unrecoverable fees being collected from an applicant receiving
no capacity allocation from Batch Zero.

        Imposing a non-refundable fee is inequitable and inappropriate prior to full assurance of a
specified capacity allocation, as it requires payment for nothing in return. Projects that are
submitted for Batch Zero Studied Load are not required to provide the non-refundable fee until the
Batch Study is complete, and capacity allocations have been assured, much later in the process
(estimated February or March of 2027). The non-refundable fee requirement in July for projects
whose studies are invalidated is inconsistent with cost causation principles, as there is no
relationship between the non-refundable fee imposed and the costs caused by the large load.

       Further, this very significant and early forfeiture of capital could occur solely because
ERCOT exercises its discretion to invalidate already completed studies, creating outsized risk to a
prospective large load. Those large loads who submit information to be considered Batch Zero
Base Load and that are later recategorized to Studied Load on the basis of this validation decision
may potentially receive allocations of zero MW in the Batch Zero Study process, effectively
paying millions of dollars in exchange for nothing. This is inappropriate, discriminatory, and does
not support business development, minimize stranded costs, or impact reliability.

       Therefore, the PUCT should guide ERCOT to:

                i. Make any non-refundable fee only refundable to a large load if ERCOT deems
                   the large load to not be Batch Zero Base Load.
               ii. Require any PUCT-approved non-refundable fee to be imposed at the time of
                   signing the Interconnection Agreement after the Batch Study is completed.

VI.    Adjust Security Refundability to be Cost-based

         Section 25.194(d)(10)(E) states the refund of security is “subject to subsections (g) through
(i) of this section.” This section is completely unjustified. Comments by ERCOT at the March 30th
ERCOT Batch Process workshop indicated that staff is aware of this hopefully unintended
reference. Tract opposes converting a security into a penalty, especially for anything not reflecting
the real cost of an ILLE’s failure to perform. The intent of financial security should be to protect
the beneficiary from stranded costs, nothing more and nothing less. However, in this case, security
provided at the Intermediate Agreement stage could be forfeited despite all costs incurred by the

                                                  7
 TSP being deducted from that security. At this stage, the ILLE capacity request has not yet even
been evaluated in the Batch Study; it could be determined that the capacity available for allocation
is below the acceptable minimum request, or even zero MW. The ILLE would have no influence
over this determination, would be forced to withdraw, and yet, despite covering all costs incurred
by the TSP, would forfeit 80% of the leftover security to be directed to other consumers. This is
not rationally related to any costs caused by the ILLE, and this will make financial security and
project development significantly more expensive. The cost of security will increase because there
is no value received (no capacity allocation), potentially high risk of non-recovery, no
predictability of the results of the Batch Study, and no relation to performance by the ILLE of its
obligations. Events outside of the large load’s control, including delays in the utility’s construction
schedule or third-party failure to secure rights of way, could result in delays in meeting the
energization schedule – these delays would not be caused by the ILLE. This will result in added
costs from the security provider (e.g., banks) to account for the heightened risk exposure when
providing security in the first place. The carrying cost of instruments used to procure security that
is potentially 80% non-refundable for six-month delays not the fault of the ILLE will differ greatly
from those commonly used by utilities or ERCOT.

        For projects that do energize, the proposed rule requires the Interconnecting Utility to
return 20% of the remaining balance of posted financial security when the large load customer
energizes and ratably as the large load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer' s
schedule for phased energization of its contracted peak demand. The Interconnecting Utility must
then return any remaining balance when the large load customer sustains operations for five years
at the customer’s contracted peak. The return of posted financial security five years after 100%
energization is an unnecessarily long time. There are two issues of concern with this approach.
First, several parties noted in their comments that large load facilities are designed with a
maximum electrical capacity that they expect to achieve very rarely, for example, they may only
achieve that capacity on an exceptionally hot day in an unusual year. That is the nature of design;
projects are developed to handle extreme cases, and it may be years before the facility reaches its
100% peak demand. Financial security should be returned to the customer once the costs the
financial security were protecting against no longer pose a risk (e.g., stranded costs or shifting of
costs). After the initial 20% is returned to the customer upon energization, the remaining financial
security should be returned once the transmission charges paid by the interconnecting large load
exceeds the financial security provided, or within five years, whichever happens first.

        There is no cost-based reason to delay return of financial security for five years past when
transmission charges paid by the large load customer to the Interconnecting Utility equal or exceed
the financial security provided. This incentivizes full utilization of facilities and therefore reduces
the risk of stranded costs, the more the large load uses the quicker it gets its security back. The
extended timeline for refund beyond when the potential stranded costs have been recovered is also
a disincentive to do business in Texas. Financial security returned for a project which has
completed its full facility build out and paid its transmission charges is financial security that can
be used to develop additional projects and support further business development in the state that

                                                  8
 charges and refunds based on costs rather than arbitrary timelines. Tract agrees with the Data
Center Coalition that a project should receive return of its posted financial security at the end of
the proposed five years or when it has paid the cost associated with its interconnection through
those rates, whichever comes first.
VII.   Allow for Surety Bonds as Option to meet Financial Security

         The Proposal for Publication (subsections (d)(10)(C), (d)(11)(C) and (f)(10)(A)) lists the
acceptable forms for the required financial security. Tract recommends that surety bonds be added
to this list. Surety bonds are a proven method of providing financial security and are accepted by
ERCOT and other utilities and market operators across the country. This addition will meet the
dual objectives of supporting business development and lowering infrastructure costs.
VIII. Allow partial refund of security for significant equipment or services for projects

        In the case of a project not meeting its energization milestones, financial security provided
for significant equipment or services should be returned to the customer if equipment purchased
can be reused or transferred to a subsequent large load customer or other TSP/DSP operations, at
the time such later use occurs, minus a nominal cost or percentage meant to cover the facilitation
and depreciation of the equipment. This is in line with common standards for duties to mitigate
that all contractual counterparties are familiar with. Requiring a duty to mitigate would also
minimize waste and therefore minimize stranded costs. At the March 24, 2026 Batch Study Process
workshop, ERCOT and PUCT acknowledged this issue and stated they were considering changes.
Tract recommends adhering to cost-causation principles by requiring the utilities mitigate costs
then deduct all actual costs incurred by the utilities from the security. The large load customer
should receive a refund of 100% of the remaining amount.
IX.    Conclusion

       Tract appreciates consideration of these important comments as the Proposal for
Publication is being finalized.
                                                       Respectfully Submitted,




                                                              Orijit Ghoshal
                                                              Vice President, Government and
                                                              Regulatory Affairs
                                                              3200 Cherry Creek Drive
                                                              Denver, CO 80209

 X.       Executive Summary – Tract – (Project 58481)
     •   Applicability and Retroactivity: The Standards should apply only to new or expanded
         large-load interconnection requests submitted after the rule’s effective date, as required
         by Senate Bill 6. Retroactive application would conflict with statutory language,
         legislative intent, and executed agreements formed under existing rules. Projects with
         LLIS numbers, submitted studies, or executed Transmission Service Provider agreements
         should not be newly subject to the Standards. Retroactivity would increase regulatory
         uncertainty, deter investment, raise litigation risk, and unnecessarily overlap with
         ERCOT’s ongoing Batch Study Process under PGRR 145.
     •   Financial Security and Netting: Any new financial security requirements must be
         netted against security and contributions already provided. Failure to net would
         double-secure costs, violate cost-causation principles, and penalize projects that complied
         with prior rules. SB 6 contemplates a uniform interconnection entry gate, not cumulative
         security obligations.
     •   Non-Refundable Fee: A non-refundable interconnection fee is not authorized by SB 6
         and departs from cost-causation principles. A uniform $/MW fee is unrelated to
         project-specific interconnection costs and is imposed too late to deter phantom loads.
         Converting refundable security into a fee undermines SB 6’s refundability provisions.
         Any fee, if adopted, should apply only after capacity allocation is assured and provide
         value to the customer.
     •   Stranded Cost Risk: Existing safeguards—including CIAC, refundable per-megawatt
         security, long-lead-time equipment security, and upgrade security—already substantially
         mitigate stranded-cost risk. Any remaining transmission cost issues should be addressed
         in Project No. 58484. Load growth can reduce rates by spreading fixed costs, with limited
         minimum-charge mechanisms available if further protection is needed.
     •   Phantom Load Mitigation: Phantom load risk can be directly addressed by requiring
         proof of land control (deed or lease) and confirmation of local zoning approvals at the
         Interconnection Agreement stage. These measures ensure projects are legally and locally
         viable before reserving capacity and directly target phantom loads without arbitrary fees.
     •   ERCOT Batch Zero – Legacy Projects: ERCOT’s proposed retroactive study cutoffs
         conflict with prior PUCT guidance and the Planning Guide. Projects submitted by
         December 31, 2025 and accepted by July 10, 2026 should qualify as Batch Zero Base
         Load. Because RPG approval timing is beyond developer and utility control, validated
         projects should proceed under the legacy process without additional Batch Study delays.
     •   Fees and Projects Invalidated by ERCOT: Non-refundable fees should not be imposed
         before capacity allocation is assured. Projects later deemed ineligible for Batch Zero Base
         Load should not forfeit fees paid prior to validation. Any fee should be assessed only
         after Batch Study completion and Interconnection Agreement execution.
     •   Security Refundability and Forms: Financial security should be refunded based on
         actual cost recovery and should not function as a penalty for events outside a project’s
         control. Remaining security should be returned once transmission charges paid equal or
         exceed the security, or within five years. Surety bonds should be allowed, and utilities
         should mitigate costs and refund unused security where equipment is reusable.

    TRACT HOLDING COMPANY I, LLC'S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION' S
 PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION
                      STANDARDS ("STANDARDS")

I.     Introduction

       Tract Holding Company I, LLC, on behalf of its affiliates, ("Tract") appreciates the
opportunity to submit comments on key issues addressed in this rulemaking. Tract, through its
affiliates, acquires land and develops construction-ready development sites for data centers-pre-
positioning power, fiber, zoning, and entitlements-to execute the most difficult early-state
development work which provides data center constructors with faster build cycles at lower risk.
Tract is actively developing several such projects in Texas and currently has 2.8 gigawatts ("GW")
of proposed projects, representing an ultimate capacity of 6.2 GW, in advanced stages of
development in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas ("ERCOT") Large Load Interconnection
Study ("LLIS") process (comprised of four projects across three Transmission Service Providers
("TSPs")), with more in development. Tract appreciates the PUCT's process thus far and supports
several changes made by the PUCT, however, Tract identifies several issues below that make the
rule legally vulnerable or conflict with enacting legislation. Tract's affiliate, Fleet Data Centers,
recently announced a lease in Nevada with a AA- investment grade rated tenant with a market cap
in excess of $3 trillion and would like to bring similar business development to Texas.

II.    Applicability

        Tract requests the Commission clarify that these Standards only apply to new large load
requests submitted to TSPs after the effective date of the rule. Projects with executed agreements
with TSPs prior to the rule becoming effective, and whose financial parameters were set under
existing rules, should not be negatively impacted by the retroactive application of this rule. As
discussed during the Texas House State Affairs Committee Meeting April 9,2026, projects with
commitments in hand were not intended to be the target of this new rule. Through Senate Bill 6
(2025 Reg. Ses.) ("SB 6"), the Texas Legislature and Governor evinced their intent by explicitly
stating that "the standards must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded
interconnection." Texas Utilities Code § 37.0561(c). This plain language would require the new
Standards be applied only to proj ects requesting "new or expanded" interconnection after the date
of adoption of the rule implementing the statute. The plain language of SB 6 also states that these

                                                  1
 are Standards the PUCT must implement by rule; they are not requirements applicable as of the
effective date ofthe underlying bill (i.e. June 20,2025) or some other date (e.g. September 1,2025,
which is a date applicable to the net metering review requirements). Texas Utilities Code §
37.0561(b).

        When serious projects begin the process of entering the ERCOT market, significant
decisions, including financial resource commitments, are made based on the rules in place at the
time. To change these rules for proj ects already in advanced stages of development will have a
negative impact on businesses and send a harmful market signal that will deter future business
development and will create overall regulatory uncertainty, counter to the intent of SB 6. If the
Commission believes it must apply these Standards to existing load interconnection requests,
contrary to the plain language of SB 6, the new Standards adopted by this rule should not apply to
projects that are so far along that they have already been assigned an LLIS number by ERCOT, or
have studies submitted to ERCOT by the TSP, or at the very least have executed agreements with
the TSP to provide financial security or contributions. Without such clarification, this rule could
 conflict with executed agreements, change terms of existing contracts, and therefore be subj ect to
judicial challenge by an aggrieved counterparty. Upsetting contractual relationships should be a
last resort.

        Moreover, applying these Standards only to newly submitted requests after the adoption
date has the added benefit of avoiding confusion with the ongoing Batch Study Process ERCOT
is developing through PGRR145. The Batch Zero criteria and batching process will be applied to
both existing and new requests going forward, while these Standards would apply only to new
requests submitted after the Standards are adopted. Doing so avoids confusion and reduces the
burden and complexity faced by developers, utilities, PUCT, and ERCOT that would result if
existing requests are required to meet the Batch requirements by July in addition to these Standards
whenever they become effective. In light of the above, Tract respectfully recommends changes to
the applicability section of the Standards to reflect the rule only applies to requests submitted to a
TSP after the effective date of this rule.

       In contrast, retroactively introducing new burdens on late-stage proj ects imposes additional
costs, can create delays, and will potentially harm businesses, strand investment, and discourage
future investment in the state, contrary to the goals of SB 6. This rulemaking process itself should
not become a cause of delay in projects moving forward. Tract is especially concerned that the
new rule imposes costs or burdens on projects previously studied or in the process of being studied
and most certainly for those projects that have already executed agreements with TSPs on the basis
of the old rules.

       Thus, Tract also respectfully recommends changes to sections addressing financial security
to recognize the contributions and financial securities provided by proj ects to date. As Chairman
Gleason himself noted at the House State Affairs Committee Meeting, projects with existing
agreements with their TSPs under that have provided financial security or contributions will have


                                                  2
 to be treated differently than those that have not. Specifically, we recommend netting the newly
imposed requirements against already provided security and contributions. This is the only way to
avoid double-securing the same costs, which would deter business development without protecting
against any incremental risks and depart significantly from cost-causation principles. Indeed, SB6
contemplates a uniform security amount that should apply to any project seeking interconnection
to ERCOT. Netting new requirements against already provided security ensures a uniform entry
gate, whereas if not netted, those early businesses who acted responsibly to secure utility costs
ahead of requirements to do so will be subj ect to newly imposed uniform requirements in addition
to already provided security and contributions. This would discriminate against and penalize
proj ects initiated prior to the rule's adoption that took prior action to protect the TSP's customers
from stranded costs.


III.    Remove non-refundable fee

        Imposing a non-refundable fee that is not tied to the costs to interconnect violates cost
causation principles and willlimit economic growth. Because the proposed non-refundable fee is
not required until the Interconnection Agreement step, this fee will not address the gating issue
against phantom loads. Furthermore, SB6 authorizes the PUCT to include all or some combination
of refundable financial security related to the size of the project ($/MW), contributions in aid of
construction ("CIAC") for direct connection costs, and security for long-lead-time equipment
outlays by the interconnecting utility. SB6 does not point to any non-refundable fees. Although it
gives the Commission additional authority in §37.0561(h)(4) to adopt additional measures
"acceptable to the commission," this does not license the Commission to depart from cost-
causation principles that are rooted in PURA.

        A uniform $/MW non-refundable fee departs from cost-causation in at least two ways.
First, given all of the securities and contributions required by the rule already, the fee cannot be
reasonably related to costs as those have already been secured by the large load through other
measures. The fee is in addition to costs. Second, a uniform fee cannot reasonably be related to
actual costs as costs vary significantly with respect to required transmission upgrades across large
loads depending on size, timing, location, and many other factors. Because SB6 does not authorize
this fee and because it is not rationally related to cost-causation, the non-refundable fee exceeds
the PUCT's authority. The non-refundable fee also makes the refundability provision of SB6
superfluous by converting the security remaining after costs into the fee. If all of the security
provided gets converted into a fee, the refundability provisions of SB6 will have no meaning. Thus,
adding the requirement for a non-refundable fee to the Standards makes the proposed rule
vulnerable to legal challenge, creating additional perceived risk for investors and regulatory and
possibly judicial uncertainty, which will negatively impact investment.

       Instead, tying required fees and security amounts to costs caused by the large load ensures
equity and prevents uneconomic projects from moving forward, thereby minimizing stranded costs
and maintaining reliability. A flat non-refundable fee does not send a price signal to the

                                                  3
 development market but rather signals a lack of support for business development. If a non-
refundable fee is adopted, it should provide some value to the large load customer, such as a
transmission service bill credit, tax credit, or some other item of value.

      At the March 24,2026, ERCOT Batch Study Process workshop, in response to opposition
to PUCT's proposed non-refundable interconnection fee, Barksdale English indicated the PUCT
would consider counter-proposals from stakeholders that: (1) minimize stranded costs; and (2)
reduce phantom loads. Tract proposes:

    1. Minimize Stranded Costs -
            a. By requiring CIAC for direct connection costs, AND $/MW security for LLE, AND
               security for long-lead-time equipment, AND security for system upgrades, this
               proposed rule already minimizes if not eliminates stranded cost risk.

            b. The direct connection and system upgrade contributions and securities alone should
               pay for any costs imposed by the large load on other ratepayers. Nevertheless, out
                 of an abundance of caution, any lingering stranded cost risk can be mitigated
                 through the proposed dollar per megawatt refundable security, which is on top of
                 actual costs identified by the utilities necessary to interconnect the large load.
                 Minimum transmission charges, as recommended by Google and Lancium (based
                 on 25% of non-coincident peak demand), could be a method to further insulate
                 against stranded cost risk in the transmission cost allocation rulemaking.

            c.   The proper venue for any further perceived transmission cost risk can be addressed
                 in Project 58484, Evaluation ofTransmission Cost Recovery, as required by Section
                 6 of SB6. Recent reports suggest that large load growth can reduce rates for other
                 customers.1 This was corroborated by Oncor's witness at the State Affairs
                 Committee Hearing who testified that for every $143 in transmission costs caused
                 by large loads they collect $146 in revenue. At that hearing, Vistra also asserted
                 that load growth would benefit its gas fleet through higher utilization. Spreading
                 fixed costs over higher volumes should lead to lower rates, which the PUCT can
                 evaluate in Project 58484.

    2. Reduce Phantom Loads -
          a. To deter phantom loads, the PUCT should require a deed or lease at the
             Interconnection Agreement stage. A purchase and sale agreement ("PSA") is
             insufficient to demonstrate a sufficiently serious project because a PSA is an
                 executory contract where the title to the land required to construct the proj ect does
                 not pass to the buyer until the deed is delivered at closing. A project has more at
                 stake and is committed to the land once it has deed in hand, which conveys the fee
                 simple estate needed for full control and financing. PSAs have provisions allowing

          justification for the March 4 date is for complete and valid LLIS studies rather than
          RPG studies. Even if the LLIS justification was also intended to encompass RPG

V.   Guide ERCOT on Large Loads whose Studies are invalidated by ERCOT


                                                6
         If PUCT adopts a non-refundable fee, the non-refundable fee should not apply to large
loads that are seeking to enter Batch Zero as base load, but could apply to those large loads whose
studies are invalidated by ERCOT. After a project submits the non-refundable fee in July as base
load, ERCOT may, in August, deem the studies associated with a proj ect invalid. In contrast, large
loads entering the Batch Zero process in July as Studied Load will not be required to post non-
refundable fees until they have received fixed capacity allocation commitments through the
ERCOT process. At the March 24,2026 Batch Zero workshop, ERCOT acknowledged this issue
and stated that it was considering changes. Failure to resolve this mismatch of funding and
commitment could result in huge unrecoverable fees being collected from an applicant receiving
no capacity allocation from Batch Zero.

        Imposing a non-refundable fee is inequitable and inappropriate prior to full assurance of a
specified capacity allocation, as it requires payment for nothing in return. Projects that are
submitted for Batch Zero Studied Load are not required to provide the non-refundable fee until the
Batch Study is complete, and capacity allocations have been assured, much later in the process
(estimated February or March of 2027). The non-refundable fee requirement in July for proj ects
whose studies are invalidated is inconsistent with cost causation principles, as there is no
relationship between the non-refundable fee imposed and the costs caused by the large load.

       Further, this very significant and early forfeiture of capital could occur solely because
ERCOT exercises its discretion to invalidate already completed studies, creating outsized risk to a
prospective large load. Those large loads who submit information to be considered Batch Zero
Base Load and that are later recategorized to Studied Load on the basis of this validation decision
may potentially receive allocations of zero MW in the Batch Zero Study process, effectively
paying millions of dollars in exchange for nothing. This is inappropriate, discriminatory, and does
not support business development, minimize stranded costs, or impact reliability.

       Therefore, the PUCT should guide ERCOT to:

                i. Make any non-refundable fee only refundable to a large load if ERCOT deems
                   the large load to not be Batch Zero Base Load.
               ii. Require any PUCT-approved non-refundable fee to be imposed at the time of
                   signing the Interconnection Agreement after the Batch Study is completed.

VI.    Adjust Security Refundability to be Cost-based

         Section 25.194(d)(10)(E) states the refund of security is "subject to subsections (g) through
(i) of this section." This section is completely unjustified. Comments by ERCOT at the March 301h
ERCOT Batch Process workshop indicated that staff is aware of this hopefully unintended
reference. Tract opposes converting a security into a penalty, especially for anything not reflecting
the real cost of an ILLE's failure to perform. The intent of financial security should be to protect
the beneficiary from stranded costs, nothing more and nothing less. However, in this case, security
provided at the Intermediate Agreement stage could be forfeited despite all costs incurred by the


                                                  7
 TSP being deducted from that security. At this stage, the ILLE capacity request has not yet even
been evaluated in the Batch Study; it could be determined that the capacity available for allocation
is below the acceptable minimum request, or even zero MW. The ILLE would have no influence
over this determination, would be forced to withdraw, and yet, despite covering all costs incurred
by the TSP, would forfeit 80% of the leftover security to be directed to other consumers. This is
not rationally related to any costs caused by the ILLE, and this will make financial security and
project development significantly more expensive. The cost of security will increase because there
is no value received (no capacity allocation), potentially high risk of non-recovery, no
predictability of the results of the Batch Study, and no relation to performance by the ILLE of its
obligations. Events outside of the large load's control, including delays in the utility's construction
schedule or third-party failure to secure rights of way, could result in delays in meeting the
energization schedule - these delays would not be caused by the ILLE. This will result in added
costs from the security provider (e.g., banks) to account for the heightened risk exposure when
providing security in the first place. The carrying cost of instruments used to procure security that
is potentially 80% non-refundable for six-month delays not the fault ofthe ILLE will differ greatly
from those commonly used by utilities or ERCOT.

       For proj ects that do energize, the proposed rule requires the Interconnecting Utility to
return 20% of the remaining balance of posted financial security when the large load customer
energizes and ratably as the large load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer' s
schedule for phased energization of its contracted peak demand. The Interconnecting Utility must
then return any remaining balance when the large load customer sustains operations for five years
at the customer's contracted peak. The return of posted financial security five years after 100%
energization is an unnecessarily long time. There are two issues of concern with this approach.
First, several parties noted in their comments that large load facilities are designed with a
maximum electrical capacity that they expect to achieve very rarely, for example, they may only
achieve that capacity on an exceptionally hot day in an unusual year. That is the nature of design;
proj ects are developed to handle extreme cases, and it may be years before the facility reaches its
100% peak demand. Financial security should be returned to the customer once the costs the
financial security were protecting against no longer pose a risk (e.g., stranded costs or shifting of
costs). After the initial 20% is returned to the customer upon energization, the remaining financial
security should be returned once the transmission charges paid by the interconnecting large load
exceeds the financial security provided, or within five years, whichever happens first.

        There is no cost-based reason to delay return of financial security for five years past when
transmission charges paid by the large load customer to the Interconnecting Utility equal or exceed
the financial security provided. This incentivizes full utilization of facilities and therefore reduces
the risk of stranded costs, the more the large load uses the quicker it gets its security back. The
extended timeline for refund beyond when the potential stranded costs have been recovered is also
a disincentive to do business in Texas.       Financial security returned for a project which has
completed its full facility build out and paid its transmission charges is financial security that can
be used to develop additional proj ects and support further business development in the state that

                                                  8
 charges and refunds based on costs rather than arbitrary timelines. Tract agrees with the Data
Center Coalition that a proj ect should receive return of its posted financial security at the end of
the proposed five years or when it has paid the cost associated with its interconnection through
those rates, whichever comes first.

VII.   Allow for Surety Bonds as Option to meet Financial Security

         The Proposal for Publication (subsections (d)(10)(C), (d)(11)(C) and (f)(10)(A)) lists the
acceptable forms for the required financial security. Tract recommends that surety bonds be added
to this list. Surety bonds are a proven method of providing financial security and are accepted by
ERCOT and other utilities and market operators across the country. This addition will meet the
dual objectives of supporting business development and lowering infrastructure costs.

VIII. Allow partial refund of security for significant equipment or services for projects

       In the case of a project not meeting its energization milestones, financial security provided
for significant equipment or services should be returned to the customer if equipment purchased
can be reused or transferred to a subsequent large load customer or other TSP/DSP operations, at
the time such later use occurs, minus a nominal cost or percentage meant to cover the facilitation
and depreciation of the equipment. This is in line with common standards for duties to mitigate
that all contractual counterparties are familiar with. Requiring a duty to mitigate would also
minimize waste and therefore minimize stranded costs. At the March 24,2026 Batch Study Process
workshop, ERCOT and PUCT acknowledged this issue and stated they were considering changes.
Tract recommends adhering to cost-causation principles by requiring the utilities mitigate costs
then deduct all actual costs incurred by the utilities from the security. The large load customer
should receive a refund of 100% of the remaining amount.

IX.    Conclusion

Publication is being finalized.

 Executive Summary - Tract - (Proiect 58481)
Applicability and Retroactivity: The Standards should apply only to new or expanded
large-load interconnection requests submitted after the rule' s effective date, as required
by Senate Bill 6. Retroactive application would conflict with statutory language,
legislative intent, and executed agreements formed under existing rules. Projects with
LLIS numbers, submitted studies, or executed Transmission Service Provider agreements
should not be newly subj ect to the Standards. Retroactivity would increase regulatory
uncertainty, deter investment, raise litigation risk, and unnecessarily overlap with
ERCOT' s ongoing Batch Study Process under PGRR 145.
Financial Security and Netting: Any new financial security requirements must be
netted against security and contributions already provided. Failure to net would
double-secure costs, violate cost-causation principles, and penalize proj ects that complied
with prior rules. SB 6 contemplates a uniform interconnection entry gate, not cumulative
security obligations.
Non-Refundable Fee: A non-refundable interconnection fee is not authorized by SB 6
and departs from cost-causation principles. A uniform $/MW fee is unrelated to
proj ect-specific interconnection costs and is imposed too late to deter phantom loads.
Converting refundable security into a fee undermines SB 6' s refundability provisions.
Any fee, if adopted, should apply only after capacity allocation is assured and provide
value to the customer.
Stranded Cost Risk: Existing safeguards-including CIAC, refundable per-megawatt
security, long-lead-time equipment security, and upgrade security-already substantially
mitigate stranded-cost risk. Any remaining transmission cost issues should be addressed
in Project No. 58484. Load growth can reduce rates by spreading fixed costs, with limited
minimum-charge mechanisms available if further protection is needed.
Phantom Load Mitigation: Phantom load risk can be directly addressed by requiring
proof of land control (deed or lease) and confirmation of local zoning approvals at the
Interconnection Agreement stage. These measures ensure proj ects are legally and locally
viable before reserving capacity and directly target phantom loads without arbitrary fees.
ERCOT Batch Zero - Legacy Projects: ERCOT's proposed retroactive study cutoffs
conflict with prior PUCT guidance and the Planning Guide. Proj ects submitted by
December 31, 2025 and accepted by July 10,2026 should qualify as Batch Zero Base
Load. Because RPG approval timing is beyond developer and utility control, validated
projects should proceed under the legacy process without additional Batch Study delays.
Fees and Projects Invalidated by ERCOT: Non-refundable fees should not be imposed
before capacity allocation is assured. Projects later deemed ineligible for Batch Zero Base
Load should not forfeit fees paid prior to validation. Any fee should be assessed only
after Batch Study completion and Interconnection Agreement execution.
Security Refundability and Forms: Financial security should be refunded based on
actual cost recovery and should not function as a penalty for events outside a proj ect' s
control. Remaining security should be returned once transmission charges paid equal or
exceed the security, or within five years. Surety bonds should be allowed, and utilities
should mitigate costs and refund unused security where equipment is reusable.
